description:
Hi everyone! We are a team with backgrounds in AI, machine learning, engineering, data analysis, and project management. We are passionate about using technology to solve real-world problems, especially in healthcare and space exploration.

For this NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to develop a practical and innovative solution for monitoring astronauts' health.
summary:
Healthy Astronauts is a health companion for astronauts on long missions, built for moments when Earth is too far away to help right away.

Every morning, an astronaut can type something as simple as “heart beat is 68, slept 6 hours”, snap a photo of a device screen, and answer six quick wellbeing questions. A small AI model running on the crew’s own computer turns that into readings, with no internet needed.

Each reading is then compared with real NASA data: Apollo-era heart rate, blood pressure and blood tests, and in-flight sleep from the NASA Standard Measures study. When something looks off, the app doesn’t just flag it in red. It shows how to measure again correctly, suggests a nap after a short night, or recommends talking with a psychologist and taking a few calm minutes with meditation or music when stress runs high.

This matters because on the way to the Moon or Mars, the first person who notices a problem is usually the astronaut. Healthy Astronauts helps them notice early, understand why, and know what to do next.
details:
Healthy Astronauts helps astronauts check their own health on long missions, when Earth may be minutes away by radio. Each day, an astronaut can type a simple sentence like “heart beat is 68, slept 6 hours”, take a photo of a device screen, and answer six wellbeing questions, and a small AI model running on their own computer pulls out the readings. Each reading is compared with real NASA data: Apollo heart rate, blood pressure and blood tests, plus NASA in-flight sleep data. Where NASA has no published range, we use a clearly labelled simulated baseline.

Simple rules decide whether something needs attention, and the AI only explains the result in plain words. When a reading is off, it turns red and an animation shows how to measure it again correctly. Short sleep suggests a nap, and high stress suggests talking with a psychologist and trying meditation or music. A glowing body map, colourful trends and a mood sticker make everything easy to read at a glance.

We built it with Python for the Windows app and HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website, with a local Llama 3.2 model through Ollama and hosting on Google Cloud. We wrote the code with OpenAI Codex and Claude Code. Codex created the watermarked illustrations and animations, and Claude generated the simulated crew data and helped build the presentation. It works offline, keeps health data on the device, and is a hackathon prototype, not a medical device.
